cards.front: What are amyloid plaques in Alzheimer disease?
cards.back: Deposits of a small peptide, amyloid-β (Aβ), that build up between neurons.
cards.quote: Amyloid plaques are deposits of a small peptide, amyloid-β (Aβ), that build up between neurons in Alzheimer disease.

cards.front: In neurodegeneration research, what can each kind of evidence show: a deposit at autopsy, a disease-causing variant in families, and a randomized trial?
cards.back: Deposit: what builds up, not whether it kills. Variant: what can start the disease, not whether removing its product helps. Trial on clinical outcomes: whether changing the target helps, and its harms.
cards.quote: A deposit seen at autopsy shows what builds up, not whether it kills.
cards.section: Four questions and one idea

cards.front: For amyloid-clearing treatment in early Alzheimer disease, what have randomized trials shown so far?
cards.back: Decline slows but does not stop.
cards.quote: For amyloid in early Alzheimer disease, the answer so far is that decline slows but does not stop.
cards.section: Four questions and one idea

cards.front: {{c1::Selective vulnerability}} means that the pathology of a neurodegenerative disease strikes some neuronal populations and spares others, often close neighbours.
cards.quote: Selective vulnerability means that the pathology strikes some neuronal populations and spares others, often close neighbours
cards.section: Which neurons die: three diseases, three populations

cards.front: Which neurons are lost early in Alzheimer disease?
cards.back: Layer II neurons of the entorhinal cortex and pyramidal neurons of hippocampal field CA1, both in the circuit for new declarative memories.
cards.quote: neurons lost early include neurons of layer II of the entorhinal cortex, the main gateway between neocortex and hippocampus
cards.section: Which neurons die: three diseases, three populations

cards.front: In Parkinson disease, the defining loss is of dopamine neurons in the {{c1::substantia nigra pars compacta}} (SNpc), whose axons supply the striatum.
cards.quote: In Parkinson disease, the defining loss is of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc)
cards.section: Which neurons die: three diseases, three populations

cards.front: In ALS, where are the cell bodies of upper and of lower motor neurons?
cards.back: Upper: motor cortex, with axons in the corticospinal tract and corticobulbar projection. Lower: brainstem and ventral horn of the spinal cord, with axons to muscle. Both cell bodies and axons degenerate.
cards.quote: Upper motor neurons have their cell bodies in motor cortex and send axons down the corticospinal tract to the spinal cord
cards.section: Which neurons die: three diseases, three populations

cards.front: In ALS, lower motor neurons in the ventral horn die one by one. What happens to the muscle fibres each one supplied, and why?
cards.back: Its whole motor unit drops out: all the fibres it supplied lose their motor neuron at once.
cards.why: A motor unit is one motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it supplies.
cards.quote: As lower motor neurons die, whole motor units (one motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it supplies
cards.section: Which neurons die: three diseases, three populations

cards.front: Dopamine neurons from postmortem human substantia nigra were sorted into ten populations by the genes they express. One population, marked by AGTR1, was highly susceptible to loss in Parkinson disease. What does this show?
cards.back: Selective vulnerability works even within one cell class: "dopamine neurons" is too broad a label for what Parkinson disease kills.
cards.quote: one population, marked by expression of the gene AGTR1, was highly susceptible to loss in PD
cards.section: Which neurons die: three diseases, three populations

cards.front: Alzheimer disease has two deposits. Where does each lie, and what protein does each contain?
cards.back: Amyloid plaques: outside cells, Aβ. Neurofibrillary tangles: inside neurons, misfolded hyperphosphorylated tau, a protein that normally binds microtubules.
cards.quote: Neurofibrillary tangles lie inside neurons and contain misfolded, hyperphosphorylated tau (carrying extra phosphate groups)
cards.section: What builds up: proteins that clump

cards.front: Aβ peptides are cut from amyloid precursor protein (APP) by two enzymes, {{c1::β-secretase}} and then γ-secretase.
cards.quote: peptides cut from amyloid precursor protein (APP) by two protein-cutting enzymes, β-secretase and then γ-secretase
cards.section: What builds up: proteins that clump

cards.front: The major component of the filaments extracted from Lewy bodies in Parkinson disease is {{c1::α-synuclein}}.
cards.quote: found α-synuclein to be the major component of the filaments extracted from Lewy bodies
cards.section: What builds up: proteins that clump

cards.front: ALS in most cases has inclusions of {{c1::TDP-43}}, an RNA-binding protein that leaves the nucleus and gathers in the cytoplasm.
cards.quote: ALS in most cases has inclusions of TDP-43, an RNA-binding protein that leaves the nucleus and gathers in the cytoplasm.
cards.section: What builds up: proteins that clump

cards.front: A protein turns up in every lesion of a neurodegenerative disease. Why does that not show the protein kills the neuron?
cards.back: A deposit shows what a lesion is made of, not what kills the cell. Small soluble aggregates, loss of the protein's normal job, or the cell's response could do the damage.
cards.quote: A deposit tells you what a lesion is made of, not that it kills the cell.
cards.section: What builds up: proteins that clump

cards.front: What is the status of "prion-like spread" of misfolded seeds in neurodegenerative diseases?
cards.back: A hypothesis, tested mostly in animal and cell models. The diseases do not pass between people through ordinary contact, though rare transmission of Aβ pathology through contaminated medical material has been reported.
cards.quote: That is a hypothesis, tested mostly in animal and cell models.
cards.section: What builds up: proteins that clump

cards.front: How does a Mendelian disease variant differ from a risk allele?
cards.back: A Mendelian variant can cause the disease in families that carry it. A risk allele only shifts the odds: many carriers never get the disease and many patients lack it, so it is neither necessary nor sufficient.
cards.quote: A risk allele only shifts the odds. Many carriers never get the disease, and many patients do not carry it.
cards.section: What can start it: genes that cause and genes that raise risk

cards.front: In a pedigree, a genotype and an illness travel together (cosegregation). Why is that evidence for a cause but not proof?
cards.back: A nearby harmless variant can travel with the true one. A second unrelated family with the same pattern, and showing what the variant does, make the case much stronger.
cards.quote: It is evidence for a cause, not proof by itself, because a nearby harmless variant can travel with the true one.
cards.section: What can start it: genes that cause and genes that raise risk

cards.front: The share of people with a disease genotype who fall ill by a given age is the {{c1::penetrance}}.
cards.back: It can be incomplete. One consortium estimate for LRRK2 G2019S was 74% by age 79; other studies report lower figures.
cards.quote: The share who do by that age is the penetrance, and it can be incomplete.
cards.section: What can start it: genes that cause and genes that raise risk

cards.front: A family's ALS is caused by a mutation in SOD1, an antioxidant enzyme. Most people with ALS have TDP-43 inclusions. Predict whether this family's dying motor neurons have them.
cards.back: No. SOD1-mutant ALS cases lacked TDP-43 inclusions at autopsy, yet their motor neurons died.
cards.why: The gene that can start a disease and the protein that builds up need not be the same.
cards.quote: ALS cases with SOD1 mutations lacked TDP-43 inclusions, yet their motor neurons died.
cards.section: What can start it: genes that cause and genes that raise risk

cards.front: How do presenilin mutations in familial Alzheimer disease change Aβ production?
cards.back: They shift the γ-secretase cut toward longer forms such as Aβ42, which clump more readily, sometimes while lowering total Aβ.
cards.quote: Presenilin mutations, for example, shift the cut toward longer forms such as Aβ42, which clump more readily, sometimes while lowering the total.
cards.section: What can start it: genes that cause and genes that raise risk

cards.front: A newly found Mendelian ALS gene is reported, and patients' motor neurons show typical TDP-43 inclusions. A student concludes the gene must encode TDP-43. Is that justified?
cards.back: No. C9ORF72 repeat expansions do not encode TDP-43, yet TDP-43 inclusions are typical; SOD1 and FUS cases run the other way. Gene and deposit can part company.
cards.why: Rule from the gene table: the gene that can start a disease and the protein that builds up need not be the same.
cards.quote: so the gene that can start a disease and the protein that builds up need not be the same.
cards.section: What can start it: genes that cause and genes that raise risk

cards.front: A 70-year-old carries an APOE ε4 allele and her brother carries none. Predict what each can expect regarding late-onset Alzheimer disease.
cards.back: She has raised risk but no certainty: ε4 is not sufficient to produce clinical disease even in old age. He is not protected: many patients carry no ε4.
cards.why: A risk allele is neither necessary nor sufficient.
cards.quote: It raises the risk of late-onset AD, yet even in old age it is not sufficient to produce clinical disease
cards.section: What can start it: genes that cause and genes that raise risk

cards.front: State the amyloid cascade hypothesis and the genetic pattern behind it.
cards.back: Aβ accumulation starts a process that leads to tangles, neuron loss and dementia. All three dominant Alzheimer genes (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) act on how much Aβ is made or which lengths.
cards.quote: Aβ accumulation starts a process that leads to tangles, neuron loss and dementia.
cards.section: What can start it: genes that cause and genes that raise risk

cards.front: Mendelian genetics supports an initiating role for Aβ in familial Alzheimer disease. Which two claims does it not establish?
cards.back: That Aβ alone explains the common late-onset form, and that removing Aβ from a patient will help. The second needs direct evidence of treatment benefit, ideally from randomized trials.
cards.quote: It does not show that Aβ alone explains the common late-onset form, and it does not show that removing Aβ from a patient will help.
cards.section: What can start it: genes that cause and genes that raise risk

cards.front: A rare APP variant, A673T, reduces Aβ production and protects carriers against Alzheimer disease. A colleague says this proves an Aβ-lowering drug will help people who already have symptoms. Evaluate.
cards.back: Not justified. The variant supports lifelong lower Aβ production as protective. It does not test lowering Aβ in someone already ill, where a process under way may no longer need Aβ.
cards.why: Genetics supports lifelong protection; randomized trials in patients, judged on clinical outcomes, most directly test whether changing the target helps once disease is under way.
cards.quote: It does not show that lowering Aβ in someone who is already ill will help, which is the question the trials ask.
cards.section: A protective variant: what genetics can say about lifelong change

cards.front: Even if Aβ starts Alzheimer disease, why might removing it fail to change the course?
cards.back: A process already under way may no longer need Aβ to keep going.
cards.quote: though a process already under way may no longer need Aβ to keep going
cards.section: Does removing it help: testing amyloid in trials

cards.front: In the Clarity AD lecanemab trial, mean CDR-SB change (0 to 18, higher is worse) at 18 months was +1.21 with drug and +1.66 with placebo. Calculate the absolute difference and the relative slowing.
cards.back: Absolute: 1.66 − 1.21 = 0.45 points less worsening. Relative, with placebo as base: 0.45 / 1.66 = 0.271, about 27%.
cards.quote: Adjusted mean changes at 18 months were +1.21 points with lecanemab and +1.66 with placebo.
cards.section: Does removing it help: testing amyloid in trials

cards.front: A headline says an Alzheimer drug "slowed decline by 27%". What is the 27% a share of, and did treated people still get worse?
cards.back: A share of the placebo group's decline. Yes, the treated group still worsened on average. It is not a 27% gain in memory or a fraction of patients helped.
cards.quote: The 27% is a share of the placebo group's decline.
cards.section: Does removing it help: testing amyloid in trials

cards.front: In a hypothetical trial, a rating scale (higher is worse) rose by a mean of 3.0 points with placebo and 2.1 with drug. Give the absolute and relative slowing, and say whether the treated group improved.
cards.back: Absolute: 3.0 − 2.1 = 0.9 points. Relative: 0.9 / 3.0 = 30%. The treated group did not improve; it worsened by 2.1 points.
cards.why: With placebo worsening, any relative slowing below 100% still leaves the treated group worsening.
cards.quote: When the placebo group worsens on average, any relative slowing below 100% still leaves the treated group worsening on average.
cards.section: Does removing it help: testing amyloid in trials

cards.front: What is ARIA with edema or effusion in anti-amyloid antibody trials?
cards.back: ARIA means amyloid-related imaging abnormalities; with edema or effusion, MRI shows fluid or swelling in the brain.
cards.quote: amyloid-related imaging abnormalities seen on MRI as fluid or swelling in the brain
cards.section: What it costs

cards.front: In TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2, ARIA with edema or effusion occurred in 24.0% on donanemab and 2.1% on placebo over 76 weeks. Express the risk as a ratio, as a percentage-point gap, and as people treated per extra case.
cards.back: Ratio: 24.0 / 2.1 ≈ 11.4, about eleven times as common. Gap: 24.0 − 2.1 = 21.9 percentage points. Per extra case: 1 / 0.219 ≈ 4.6 people treated.
cards.quote: occurred in 24.0% of donanemab recipients and 2.1% on placebo
cards.section: What it costs

cards.front: Donanemab slowed decline by 35.1% on iADRS over 76 weeks in people with low or medium tau; lecanemab slowed it by 27% on CDR-SB over 18 months. Is donanemab the better drug?
cards.back: The numbers cannot rank the drugs: the scales, populations and durations differ.
cards.quote: Setting 27% beside 35.1% does not rank the drugs: the scales, populations and durations differ.
cards.section: What it costs

cards.front: What is a biomarker, and why does a slower rise in one not show clinical benefit?
cards.back: A lab or imaging measure of the disease process. Slowing the measure is not the same as slower decline in the person; benefit must be shown on clinical outcomes.
cards.quote: A slower rise in a biomarker, a lab or imaging measure of the disease process, is not the same as slower decline in the person.
cards.section: A biomarker is not a benefit

cards.front: In the A4 study of cognitively unimpaired adults with elevated amyloid, amyloid PET rose 11.6 centiloids on solanezumab and 19.3 on placebo over 240 weeks. Calculate the relative slowing of amyloid build-up. Does it show slower cognitive decline?
cards.back: (19.3 − 11.6) / 19.3 ≈ 0.40, about 40% slower build-up. No: thinking declined in both groups and the trial did not demonstrate slower decline.
cards.why: A biomarker effect alone does not establish clinical benefit.
cards.quote: So amyloid built up about 40% more slowly with the drug
cards.section: A biomarker is not a benefit

cards.front: Tofersen lowered SOD1 in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma neurofilament light in SOD1-mutant ALS, but clinical endpoints did not improve at 28 weeks. A regulator later granted accelerated approval on the neurofilament fall. What has been shown, and what is still open?
cards.back: Shown: target lowering and a biomarker change. Open: clinical benefit. The approval rests on a marker judged reasonably likely to predict benefit, and the clinical answer is still being sought.
cards.why: Randomized trials judged on clinical outcomes most directly test whether changing the target helps; biomarker changes alone do not establish clinical benefit.
cards.quote: granted tofersen accelerated approval on the basis of the fall in plasma neurofilament light
cards.section: Tofersen after 28 weeks

cards.front: Name three things none of the anti-amyloid and tofersen trials showed.
cards.back: Reversal of decline, return of lost neurons, and benefit beyond the populations and durations studied.
cards.quote: None of these trials showed reversal of decline, return of lost neurons, or benefit beyond the populations and durations studied
cards.section: What none of the trials showed

cards.front: Many earlier anti-amyloid drugs missed their endpoints and verubecestat, which blocks Aβ production, did not help people with early symptoms, while plaque-clearing antibodies slowed decline modestly. What overall conclusion about amyloid do these results support?
cards.back: A contribution of amyloid that treatment can reach, without establishing amyloid as the sole cause.
cards.why: Trial outcomes test treatment benefit; mixed results limit claims to contribution, not sole causation.
cards.quote: Together the results support a contribution of amyloid that treatment can reach, without establishing amyloid as the sole cause.
cards.section: What none of the trials showed

cards.front: When asking why some neurons fail first, how do a correlate, a manipulation in an animal model, and a mechanism needed after injury differ as evidence?
cards.back: A correlate only goes with vulnerability. A manipulation that changes disease course is stronger but holds for that model. An injury mechanism may or may not be needed in disease.
cards.quote: Changing something in an animal model and seeing the disease course change is stronger, but it holds for that model.
cards.section: Why these neurons

cards.front: What correlate may help explain why nigral dopamine neurons are more vulnerable than neighbouring dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area?
cards.back: Very large axonal arbors and high energy demand, which may contribute.
cards.quote: Nigral dopamine neurons have very large axonal arbors and high energy demand, which may contribute to their vulnerability
cards.section: Why these neurons

cards.front: In SOD1G93A mice, gamma motor neurons are spared while alpha motor neurons degenerate. Genetically reducing gamma motor neurons, and so spindle afferent activation, delayed onset and prolonged lifespan. What does this show?
cards.back: Circuit input can change how fast a vulnerable neuron dies, at least in that model.
cards.why: A manipulation in a model is stronger than a correlate but holds for that model.
cards.quote: So circuit input can change how fast a vulnerable neuron dies, at least in that model.
cards.section: Why these neurons

cards.front: After an axon is cut, the distal axon fragments in Wallerian degeneration, an active program that requires {{c1::SARM1}} in flies and mice.
cards.back: The purified TIR domain of SARM1 has intrinsic NAD+-cleaving activity.
cards.quote: an active program that requires SARM1 in flies and mice (Osterloh and colleagues, 2012)
cards.section: Why these neurons

cards.front: Sarm1 deletion protects cut axons, but in SOD1G93A ALS mice it did not improve survival or the behavioural, electrophysiological or histological outcomes measured. A colleague concludes axon degeneration does not matter in ALS. Evaluate.
cards.back: Too far. The cut result does not show chronic disease uses the same program. Motor neurons may die by another route, such as apoptosis in the cell body, or axons may be partly saved without survival gain.
cards.why: A mechanism needed after injury may or may not be needed in disease, and one SOD1 overexpression line is not human ALS.
cards.quote: The 2012 result concerns a cut; it does not show that chronic disease uses the same program.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: You retest Sarm1 loss in SOD1G93A mice. What positive control do you add, why in a separate matched cohort, and what second step guards against model-specific results?
cards.back: Cut a nerve and confirm Sarm1-null axons resist degeneration, so a negative result cannot be blamed on a failed knockout. Keep disease mice uninjured, since a cut changes motor and survival measures. Then test a second model, such as TDP-43.
cards.quote: so a negative result in disease cannot be blamed on a failed knockout
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Assume decline is linear over 18 months in Clarity AD (placebo +1.66, lecanemab +1.21 CDR-SB points). How many months of placebo decline does the 0.45-point gap equal?
cards.back: Placebo rate 1.66 / 18 ≈ 0.092 points a month; 0.45 / 0.092 ≈ 4.9 months. The figure depends on the linearity assumption.
cards.quote: the 0.45-point gap equals about 4.9 months of placebo decline (0.45 / (1.66 / 18))
cards.section: A what-if: time saved

cards.front: The smallest meaningful worsening for one person on CDR-SB is estimated at about 1 point in mild cognitive impairment. Does a 0.45-point gap between group means therefore show the drug effect is meaningless?
cards.back: No. Those thresholds apply to an individual's change, not to the gap between two group averages, so the comparison does not settle the question.
cards.quote: Those are thresholds for an individual's change, not for the gap between two group averages
cards.section: Is a 0.45-point gap meaningful?
